articles.title: AI, ML, and Deep Learning: The Map You Wish You Had
articles.subtitle: Three buzzwords, one simple picture, and why the difference actually matters

glossary.definition: The broad goal of making computers do things that would seem intelligent if a person did them, like reasoning, recognizing images or understanding language.
A way of building AI where the computer learns patterns from examples instead of following rules a human wrote by hand.
Machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers, which can learn useful features straight from raw data like pixels or text.
The thing that gets learned: a function with adjustable numbers inside it that turns an input (an email, a photo) into an output (spam or not, cat or dog).
The process of showing a model many examples and nudging its internal numbers so its answers get better.
A model built from many simple connected units, loosely inspired by neurons, that pass numbers to each other in layers.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes how the three terms relate?
options: They are three names for the same thing
Deep learning is a kind of machine learning, which is one way of doing AI
AI is a kind of deep learning
Machine learning and deep learning are unrelated fields
quiz.explain: Think nesting dolls: AI is the biggest doll, machine learning sits inside it, and deep learning sits inside machine learning.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between traditional programming and machine learning?
options: Machine learning needs no data at all
Traditional programs are always faster
In machine learning you give examples and answers, and the computer works out the rules
Machine learning only works on images
quiz.explain: A programmer writes rules by hand. In machine learning, the rules are learned from examples that already have the right answers.

quiz.q: Why did deep learning become so popular after 2012?
options: Because it removed the need for computers
Because large datasets and fast GPUs let many-layered networks learn their own features
Because rule-based systems were banned
Because it needs fewer examples than any other method
quiz.explain: Deep networks are hungry for data and computation. Once both became available, they started beating hand-designed approaches.

articles.title: What Machines Actually Learn From
articles.subtitle: Data, features and labels: the raw ingredients behind every AI system you will ever meet

glossary.definition: A collection of examples that a model learns from, often stored like a big spreadsheet.
One row of a dataset: a single house, email, photo or patient the model can learn from.
One measurable property of an example, turned into a number, like a house's area or a mango's softness.
The correct answer attached to an example, which the model tries to predict, like the price of a house or whether an email is spam.
A prediction task where the answer is a category, such as spam or not spam, cat or dog.
A prediction task where the answer is a number on a scale, such as a price or a temperature.

quiz.q: In a dataset of houses, which of these is most likely the label?
options: Number of bedrooms
Distance to the metro
Selling price
Floor area
quiz.explain: The label is the thing you want to predict. Bedrooms, distance and area are features that help predict the price.

quiz.q: Predicting tomorrow's temperature in degrees is an example of what kind of task?
options: Classification
Regression
Clustering
It is not machine learning
quiz.explain: The answer is a number on a continuous scale, which makes it regression.

quiz.q: Why must every feature eventually become a number?
options: Because numbers look more scientific
Because models are mathematical functions that can only multiply and add numbers
Because text is illegal in datasets
Because labels are always numbers
quiz.explain: A model is math: it multiplies, adds and compares numbers. Words, pixels and categories all have to be encoded as numbers first.

articles.title: How Wrong Is the Model?
articles.subtitle: The single number every AI system is secretly trying to shrink

glossary.definition: A formula that takes the model's predictions and the true labels and returns one number saying how wrong the model is. Lower is better.
The model's output for an example: its guess at the label.
A loss for numeric predictions: square each error, then average them. Big mistakes count much more than small ones.
A loss for predicted probabilities. It is small when the model gives high probability to the right answer and huge when it is confident and wrong.
One of the adjustable numbers inside a model. Training means finding parameter values that make the loss small.

quiz.q: Why do we square errors in mean squared error instead of just adding them up?
options: Squaring makes the numbers smaller
So positive and negative errors cannot cancel out, and big errors count more
Because computers cannot add negative numbers
Squaring is required by law in statistics
quiz.explain: An error of +10 and one of -10 would add to zero. Squaring makes both 100 and also punishes large mistakes far more than small ones.

quiz.q: A model says 'cat' with 99% confidence, but the photo is a dog. What does cross-entropy do?
options: Gives a tiny penalty, because the model was confident
Gives no penalty
Gives a very large penalty, because the model was confident and wrong
Crashes
quiz.explain: Cross-entropy uses the probability given to the true answer. Here the dog got only 1%, and the negative log of 0.01 is large.

quiz.q: What does a model 'want' during training?
options: The highest possible loss
A loss of exactly 1
The lowest possible loss
A loss equal to the number of examples
quiz.explain: Training adjusts the parameters to make the loss as small as possible.

articles.title: Finding the Bottom of a Valley Blindfolded
articles.subtitle: Gradient descent: the humble walking algorithm that trains almost every AI model

glossary.definition: The slope of the loss with respect to each parameter. It points in the direction where the loss rises fastest.
A training method that repeatedly nudges every parameter a small step in the direction that lowers the loss.
The size of each step in gradient descent. Too small and training crawls; too large and it overshoots or blows up.
A number that says how much a function's output changes when you nudge its input a tiny bit, in other words its slope at that point.
A small random handful of training examples used to estimate the gradient for one step, instead of using the whole dataset.
A low point in the loss landscape that is lower than everything nearby but not necessarily the lowest point overall.

quiz.q: In gradient descent, which way do you step?
options: In the direction of the gradient
Opposite to the gradient, downhill
In a random direction each time
Always to the right
quiz.explain: The gradient points uphill, where the loss increases fastest. Stepping the opposite way lowers the loss.

quiz.q: What usually happens if the learning rate is far too large?
options: Training becomes perfectly accurate
Steps overshoot the valley, and the loss can bounce around or explode
The model stops using data
Nothing changes
quiz.explain: Huge steps leap over the bottom of the valley, sometimes landing higher than where they started.

quiz.q: Why do most modern models use mini-batches?
options: Because a few examples give a cheap, good-enough estimate of the slope, so you can take many more steps
Because using all the data is mathematically wrong
Because mini-batches remove the need for a loss function
Because GPUs cannot store whole datasets in principle
quiz.explain: Computing the exact gradient over millions of examples is slow. A small random batch gives a noisy but useful estimate, so training makes progress much faster.

articles.title: Yes or No? How Machines Make Decisions
articles.subtitle: Logistic regression: a weighted vote, a smooth squash, and the first real classifier you can build by hand

glossary.definition: A simple classifier that adds up weighted features into a score, then squashes the score into a probability between 0 and 1.
A number that says how strongly a feature pushes the decision, and in which direction. Weights are the parameters a classifier learns.
An extra learned number added to the score that shifts the decision up or down regardless of the features.
An S-shaped function that turns any number into a value between 0 and 1, so a score can be read as a probability.
The line (or surface) that separates the region where the model says yes from the region where it says no.
The cut-off probability for saying yes, usually 0.5, which can be moved to make the model more cautious or more eager.

quiz.q: What does the sigmoid function do in logistic regression?
options: It picks the best features automatically
It squashes any score into a value between 0 and 1
It removes the need for training
It sorts the examples by size
quiz.explain: The sigmoid maps big positive scores close to 1, big negative scores close to 0, and a score of 0 to exactly 0.5.

quiz.q: A feature has a large negative weight. What does that mean?
options: The feature is ignored
Higher values of that feature push the prediction toward 'no'
Higher values push the prediction toward 'yes'
The model is broken
quiz.explain: The weight multiplies the feature. A negative weight means more of that feature lowers the score, which lowers the probability of 'yes'.

quiz.q: Why can't plain logistic regression solve every classification problem?
options: It can only draw straight-line boundaries between classes
It needs more than two features
It cannot output probabilities
It only works on images
quiz.explain: Its decision boundary is always a straight line (or flat surface). Some patterns need curved boundaries, which is where neural networks come in.

articles.title: Memorizing vs Learning
articles.subtitle: Overfitting, underfitting and test sets: how to tell if a model actually understands anything

glossary.definition: When a model learns the training examples too closely, including their noise and quirks, so it does well on them but badly on new data.
When a model is too simple to capture the real pattern, so it does badly even on the training data.
A model's ability to perform well on new examples it never saw during training. This is the actual goal of machine learning.
The examples the model learns from.
A separate set of examples used during development to compare models and choose settings, without touching the final test.
Examples locked away until the very end and used once to measure how well the finished model generalizes.
Any technique that discourages a model from becoming too complex, so it learns the general pattern instead of memorizing.

quiz.q: A model gets 99% accuracy on training data and 60% on new data. What is most likely happening?
options: Underfitting
Overfitting
Perfect generalization
The test set is too large
quiz.explain: A big gap between training and test performance is the classic sign of overfitting: the model memorized instead of learning.

quiz.q: Why should the test set be used only once, at the very end?
options: Because it is expensive to load
Because if you keep tuning against it, it stops being an honest measure of performance on unseen data
Because models cannot read test data twice
Because it contains no labels
quiz.explain: Every decision you make by peeking at test results leaks information into the model, making the score look better than real-world performance.

quiz.q: Which of these usually helps reduce overfitting?
options: Making the model much bigger with no other change
Training on fewer examples
Getting more training data or adding regularization
Evaluating only on the training set
quiz.explain: More data makes memorizing harder, and regularization pushes the model toward simpler, more general patterns.

articles.title: Neural Networks from One Neuron Up
articles.subtitle: How stacking thousands of tiny calculators produces something that can see, read and talk

glossary.definition: The basic unit of a neural network: it multiplies its inputs by weights, adds them up with a bias, and passes the result through an activation function.
A learned number on a connection that says how strongly one input influences a neuron.
A simple non-linear function applied to a neuron's sum, such as ReLU or sigmoid. Without it, stacking layers would add no power.
Rectified Linear Unit: the activation function max(0, z). It keeps positive numbers and turns negatives into zero.
A group of neurons that all read the same inputs and pass their outputs on together to the next group.
Any layer between the input and the output. Its neurons learn intermediate features that nobody labeled.

quiz.q: What does a single artificial neuron compute?
options: A random number
A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function
The average of all training examples
A copy of its input
quiz.explain: Multiply, add, then apply a simple non-linear function. That is the whole job of one neuron.

quiz.q: Why do neural networks need non-linear activation functions like ReLU?
options: To make training slower
Because without them, many stacked layers collapse into the power of a single straight-line model
Because computers cannot multiply without them
To keep all outputs positive for display
quiz.explain: Stacking purely linear steps gives another linear step. The bends added by activation functions are what let networks learn curved boundaries.

quiz.q: What do hidden layers learn?
options: The labels, which are copied in by humans
Intermediate features that help the final prediction, discovered automatically during training
Nothing; they only pass data through
The learning rate
quiz.explain: Nobody tells hidden neurons what to detect. Training shapes them into useful feature detectors, like edges in an image.

articles.excerpt: Each artificial neuron in a neural network does something a ten-year-old could do with a pencil: multiply a few numbers, add them up, and decide whether the result is worth passing on. That is all. There is no magic inside. And yet, wire up a few million of these little calculators in the right…

articles.title: Backpropagation Without the Scary Math
articles.subtitle: How a network figures out which of its million knobs to blame for a mistake

glossary.definition: The algorithm that computes the gradient of the loss for every weight in a network by passing blame backward from the output, layer by layer.
Running inputs through the network, layer by layer, to get a prediction and a loss.
Going from the loss back toward the inputs, computing how much each weight contributed to the error.
The calculus rule that says the effect of a change passing through several steps is the product of each step's local effect.
For each weight, the slope of the loss: how much the loss would change if that weight were nudged up a little.
A problem in deep networks where blame signals shrink as they travel backward through many layers, so early layers barely learn.

quiz.q: What does backpropagation actually compute?
options: The final prediction
The gradient of the loss with respect to every weight
The best learning rate
Which training examples to delete
quiz.explain: Backpropagation is a fast way to get all the slopes. Gradient descent then uses those slopes to update the weights.

quiz.q: Why is backpropagation so much faster than nudging each weight one at a time to see what happens?
options: It skips half the weights
It reuses shared intermediate results, so one backward pass gives the slopes for all weights at once
It uses smaller numbers
It only works on tiny networks
quiz.explain: Nudging each weight separately needs a full run of the network per weight. Backprop gets every slope for roughly the cost of one extra pass.

quiz.q: What is the vanishing gradient problem?
options: Gradients become too large and overflow
Blame signals shrink as they are multiplied backward through many layers, so early layers learn very slowly
The loss disappears
Weights are deleted during training
quiz.explain: Multiplying many numbers smaller than 1 gives a tiny number. Early layers get almost no signal to learn from.

articles.title: How Words Become Numbers With Meaning
articles.subtitle: Embeddings: the map of meaning hiding inside every search engine, recommender and chatbot

glossary.definition: A list of numbers that represents a word, product, image or anything else, learned so that similar things get similar lists.
An ordered list of numbers, which you can also picture as a point or an arrow in space.
Representing an item as a long list of zeros with a single 1 in its own position. Simple, but it says nothing about meaning.
One position in a vector. A 300-dimensional embedding is a list of 300 numbers.
A score from -1 to 1 that measures how closely two vectors point in the same direction. Close to 1 means very similar.
The words that appear around a word. Embeddings are usually learned from context.

quiz.q: What is the main problem with one-hot encoding for words?
options: It uses too few numbers
Every word is equally different from every other word, so it captures no meaning
It cannot be stored on a computer
It only works for English
quiz.explain: In one-hot form, 'cat' is exactly as far from 'kitten' as it is from 'volcano'. There is no notion of similarity.

quiz.q: How do models usually learn word embeddings?
options: Linguists type in the numbers by hand
From the contexts words appear in: words used in similar contexts get similar vectors
By sorting words alphabetically
From the length of each word
quiz.explain: This is the idea that you can know a word by the company it keeps. Shared contexts pull vectors together.

quiz.q: In a good embedding space, what might king minus man plus woman land closest to?
options: Prince
Queen
Castle
Man
quiz.explain: Directions in the space can capture relationships. Removing 'male' and adding 'female' to king moves you toward queen.

articles.title: How to Read a Research Paper Without Falling Asleep
articles.subtitle: The three-pass method researchers actually use, and the five questions that unlock any paper

glossary.definition: The short paragraph at the top of a paper that summarises the problem, the method and the main result.
An existing method that a new paper compares itself against. A result only means something relative to good baselines.
A standard dataset and scoring method that many papers use, so their results can be compared fairly.
An experiment that removes one part of a method at a time to see how much each part actually matters.
The best published result on a benchmark at a given time, often shortened to SOTA.
A paper posted publicly, usually on arXiv, before or without formal peer review.
The process where other experts judge a paper before a conference or journal accepts it.

quiz.q: What is the goal of the first pass through a paper?
options: Check every equation carefully
Get the big picture in a few minutes: what problem, what idea, what result
Reimplement the method in code
Read every reference
quiz.explain: The first pass is a quick skim of the title, abstract, introduction, headings, figures and conclusion, so you can decide whether to go deeper.

quiz.q: What does an ablation study tell you?
options: How fast the method runs
How much each component of the method contributes, by removing them one at a time
Who reviewed the paper
Which dataset is largest
quiz.explain: If removing a component barely changes the result, that component was not doing much.

quiz.q: A paper reports a big improvement but only compares against weak, outdated baselines. What should you think?
options: The result is definitely groundbreaking
Be cautious: the improvement may shrink against strong, current methods
Baselines do not matter
The paper must be fake
quiz.explain: A gain is only as meaningful as the baseline it beats. Strong, fair baselines make a claim far more convincing.

articles.title: Can Machines Think? Turing's Brilliant Dodge
articles.subtitle: How a 1950 thought experiment replaced an unanswerable question with a game, and predicted learning machines
articles.paper_title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence

glossary.definition: Turing's test: a judge chats by text with a hidden human and a hidden machine and tries to tell which is which.
A machine that follows a stored list of precise instructions, step by step. Turing argued one machine could imitate any other such machine.
Turing's idea that a single computer, given the right program, can carry out any procedure that any other computer can.
Turing's proposal to build a simple machine that learns from experience and teaching, instead of programming an adult mind directly.
The argument, from Ada Lovelace's 1843 notes, that a machine can only do what we tell it and can never originate anything.

quiz.q: Why did Turing replace 'Can machines think?' with the imitation game?
options: Because he believed machines could never think
Because 'think' is too vague to answer, while a game has a clear, testable outcome
Because he wanted to build a chess computer
Because the journal required a game
quiz.explain: Turing called the original question too meaningless to deserve discussion and swapped it for something you could actually test.

quiz.q: What did Turing suggest instead of programming an adult mind directly?
options: Copying a human brain cell by cell
Building a child machine that learns through teaching and experience
Waiting for faster computers
Using only logic rules
quiz.explain: He proposed simulating a child's mind and educating it, an early sketch of machine learning.

quiz.q: What is the main criticism of the Turing test as a measure of intelligence?
options: It is too hard for any machine to ever pass
It measures how well a machine imitates human conversation, which is not the same as understanding
It requires a physical robot
It only works in English
quiz.explain: Critics argue a system could fool judges through clever imitation without genuinely understanding anything.

articles.title: The Machine That Learned From Its Mistakes
articles.subtitle: Rosenblatt's perceptron: the 1958 invention that started neural networks, and the hype that nearly ended them
articles.paper_title: The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain

glossary.definition: Rosenblatt's learning machine: it adds up weighted inputs and outputs yes if the total passes a threshold, and it adjusts its weights after every mistake.
A number on each input connection that says how strongly that input pushes the decision.
An all-or-nothing activation: output 1 if the input is above zero, otherwise 0.
After a wrong answer, add the input to the weights if the answer should have been yes, and subtract it if it should have been no.
Describes data where a single straight line (or flat surface) can perfectly separate the two classes.
A period when interest and funding for AI research collapsed after promises went unmet.

quiz.q: When does the perceptron change its weights?
options: After every example, even correct ones
Only when it makes a mistake
Never, they are fixed by hand
Only at the end of training
quiz.explain: The learning rule only fires on errors: no mistake, no change.

quiz.q: What did Minsky and Papert's 1969 book famously show?
options: That perceptrons can learn any function
That single-layer perceptrons cannot learn some simple patterns, such as XOR
That neural networks need GPUs
That the brain uses backpropagation
quiz.explain: A single perceptron can only draw a straight-line boundary, so patterns like XOR are out of reach.

quiz.q: What does the perceptron convergence theorem guarantee?
options: The perceptron always finds the best possible boundary
If the data is linearly separable, the learning rule will find a separating line in a finite number of steps
The perceptron never makes mistakes
Training takes exactly 50 steps
quiz.explain: When a straight-line separator exists, the simple correct-on-mistakes rule is guaranteed to find one eventually.

articles.title: Four Pages That Woke Up Neural Networks
articles.subtitle: How backpropagation taught hidden layers to invent their own features, and ended the perceptron's long winter
articles.paper_title: Learning Representations by Back-propagating Errors

glossary.definition: A neuron that is neither an input nor an output. Its job is not specified by anyone; it learns whatever helps.
The method of computing how much every weight contributed to the error by sending error signals backward through the network, layer by layer.
The pattern of activity across hidden units for a given input: the network's own learned description of that input.
The calculus rule that the effect of a change through several steps is the product of each step's local effect.
A training trick that lets each weight update carry along part of the previous update, smoothing and speeding up the descent.
A point where the error is lower than everywhere nearby but not the lowest possible, where gradient descent can get stuck.

quiz.q: What was the key problem that stopped multi-layer perceptrons from being trained before backpropagation became widely known?
options: Computers could not store weights
Nobody had a practical way to decide how to adjust the weights of hidden units
There was no training data
Hidden layers were illegal in neural network theory
quiz.explain: Hidden units have no target values of their own, so it was unclear how to correct them. Backpropagation computes exactly how much each one contributed to the error.

quiz.q: What did the family-tree experiment demonstrate?
options: That networks can memorize names
That hidden units spontaneously learned meaningful features such as nationality and generation that nobody had labeled
That backpropagation is faster than humans
That family trees are linearly separable
quiz.explain: The network was only given relationship facts, yet its hidden units came to encode useful properties of the people, an early demonstration of representation learning.

quiz.q: Which limitation did the authors openly acknowledge?
options: Gradient descent can get stuck in local minima, and the method is probably not how the brain learns
The method only works on images
The method cannot use hidden units
It requires quantum computers
quiz.explain: They noted that the error surface can contain local minima and that the procedure is not a plausible model of learning in real brains.

articles.title: Draw the Widest Road Between Two Crowds
articles.subtitle: Support vector machines: the margin idea that dominated machine learning before deep learning took over
articles.paper_title: Support-Vector Networks

glossary.definition: The width of the empty gap between the decision boundary and the closest training points of either class.
A training point that sits on the edge of the margin, or inside it. Only these points determine where the boundary goes.
A margin that allows some points to be on the wrong side, with a penalty, so messy real-world data can still be separated.
A number for each training point that measures how far it breaks the margin rule. Zero for well-behaved points.
A way to get the effect of mapping data into a much higher-dimensional space without ever computing that mapping directly.
The space the data lives in after a transformation; a straight boundary there can correspond to a curved one in the original space.

quiz.q: Among all lines that separate two classes, which one does an SVM choose?
options: The first one it finds
The one with the widest empty margin to the nearest points
The one that passes through the most points
The steepest line
quiz.explain: A wide margin leaves room for new points to land on the correct side, which tends to generalize better.

quiz.q: Why does the soft margin matter?
options: It makes the boundary curved
Real data is noisy and often not perfectly separable, so the model must be allowed some penalised mistakes
It removes the need for training data
It speeds up the GPU
quiz.explain: Cortes and Vapnik's soft margin lets some points violate the margin at a cost controlled by a parameter C.

quiz.q: What does the kernel trick allow?
options: Training without labels
Learning curved boundaries by implicitly working in a richer feature space, without computing it directly
Using fewer support vectors than training points is forbidden
Replacing the margin with a neural network
quiz.explain: Kernels compute similarities as if the data had been mapped into a high-dimensional space where a straight boundary works.

articles.title: Why a Crowd of Bad Guessers Beats an Expert
articles.subtitle: Breiman's random forests: deliberately weakened decision trees that vote their way to excellent predictions
articles.paper_title: Random Forests

glossary.definition: A model that makes predictions by asking a series of yes-or-no questions about the features, like a flowchart.
A group of models whose predictions are combined, usually by voting or averaging, to get a better overall prediction.
A new training set made by drawing examples at random from the original data, with replacement, so some appear twice and others not at all.
Short for bootstrap aggregating: train each model on a different bootstrap sample and combine their votes.
An error estimate computed by testing each tree only on the examples left out of its bootstrap sample, giving a free built-in test set.
A measure of how much a model relies on each feature, for example by scrambling that feature and seeing how much worse predictions get.

quiz.q: Why does a random forest add randomness when growing each tree?
options: To make each tree more accurate on its own
To make the trees different from each other, so their mistakes do not line up
To speed up the computer's clock
Randomness is a bug that Breiman could not remove
quiz.explain: Voting only helps if the voters make different mistakes. Random samples and random feature choices decorrelate the trees.

quiz.q: What happens to a random forest's test error as you keep adding more trees?
options: It rises sharply because the forest overfits
It settles down to a limit instead of getting worse
It becomes exactly zero
It oscillates forever
quiz.explain: Breiman showed that the error converges as trees are added. More trees cost time, but they do not cause overfitting.

quiz.q: What is out-of-bag error?
options: Errors caused by missing data
An error estimate that tests each tree on the examples it never saw during its own training
The error on the training data
The error from the largest tree
quiz.explain: Each bootstrap sample leaves out roughly a third of the examples, and those left-out examples act as a built-in test set.

articles.title: The Folk Wisdom Textbooks Forgot to Teach

glossary.definition: The family of models a learner can express, such as decision trees, linear models or neural networks.
A model's tendency to consistently learn the same wrong thing, usually because it is too simple.
A model's tendency to learn random things that change with the particular training data it happened to see.
The way many things that work in low dimensions break down as the number of features grows, because the space becomes vast and data becomes sparse.
The human work of designing good input features from raw data, often the deciding factor in classic machine learning projects.
A result showing that, averaged over all possible problems, no learner beats random guessing; every learner must make assumptions to succeed.

quiz.q: According to Domingos, what is the fundamental goal of machine learning?
options: To get perfect accuracy on the training data
To generalize beyond the examples in the training set
To use the most complex model available
To minimise training time
quiz.explain: Doing well on training data is easy and almost meaningless. Generalizing to new examples is the whole point.

quiz.q: What does 'more data beats a cleverer algorithm' mean in practice?
options: Algorithms do not matter at all
A simple learner with lots of data often beats a sophisticated one with little data
You should never change your algorithm
Data is cheaper than electricity
quiz.explain: Given the choice, adding data is often the most reliable way to improve. Domingos also warns that it brings the challenge of scalability.

quiz.q: Why does intuition fail in high dimensions?
options: Computers cannot store high-dimensional data
As features multiply, data becomes extremely sparse and notions like 'nearby' behave very differently from our 3D experience
High-dimensional data is always random
Humans are bad at arithmetic
quiz.explain: This is the curse of dimensionality: the space grows so fast that even huge datasets cover only a tiny fraction of it.

glossary.definition: Sliding a small grid of weights (a filter) across an image and computing a weighted sum at every position, producing a map of where a pattern appears.
A small learned grid of weights, such as 5 by 5, that responds strongly to one kind of local pattern, like an edge at a certain angle.
The output of applying one filter across a whole image: a grid showing how strongly the pattern appears at each location.
Using the same filter weights at every position in the image, so a pattern is detected wherever it appears and far fewer parameters are needed.
Shrinking a feature map by summarising small neighbourhoods, for example by averaging, which makes the network less sensitive to exact positions.
A dataset of 70,000 small images of handwritten digits, introduced in this paper, that became the classic first benchmark in machine learning.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of weight sharing in a convolutional network?
options: It makes every neuron different
The same pattern detector works anywhere in the image, with far fewer parameters
It removes the need for training
It makes images larger
quiz.explain: A filter that detects a loop in the top corner also detects it in the bottom corner, and you only store its weights once.

quiz.q: Why did LeCun argue against hand-designed feature extractors?
options: They were illegal
Learned features, trained end to end with gradient descent, could outperform features engineers designed by hand
Hand-designed features were too fast
Computers could not run them
quiz.explain: The paper's thesis is that systems trained end to end with gradient-based learning beat pipelines of hand-crafted components.

quiz.q: What does pooling (subsampling) contribute?
options: It adds more parameters
It shrinks feature maps and makes the network tolerant to small shifts and distortions
It converts images to text
It labels the data
quiz.explain: Summarising small neighbourhoods means a stroke moved by a pixel or two still produces almost the same output.

articles.title: How to Squeeze a Picture Into Thirty Numbers
articles.subtitle: Hinton and Salakhutdinov's deep autoencoders: the 2006 trick that made deep networks trainable again

glossary.definition: A network trained to reproduce its own input at its output after squeezing it through a narrow middle layer.
The first half of an autoencoder, which compresses the input down to a short code.
The second half of an autoencoder, which rebuilds the input from the short code.
The small set of numbers in the narrow middle layer: the compressed description of the input.
A classic method (PCA) that compresses data by projecting it onto the few straight-line directions with the most variation.
Training a network's layers one at a time on unlabeled data to get good starting weights before fine-tuning the whole network.
A two-layer network that learns to model the patterns in its input. The paper stacked these to pretrain each layer.

quiz.q: What is an autoencoder trained to do?
options: Classify images into labels
Reproduce its own input after squeezing it through a narrow middle layer
Generate random noise
Sort data alphabetically
quiz.explain: The target is the input itself, so no labels are needed. The narrow middle forces the network to find a compact code.

quiz.q: Why couldn't deep autoencoders simply be trained with backpropagation from random weights?
options: Backpropagation was not invented yet
From random starting weights, training tended to get stuck in poor solutions, such as outputting the average input
They had too few parameters
Computers could not do multiplication
quiz.explain: With many layers and random weights, gradients were weak and training found bad solutions. Good starting weights fixed this.

quiz.q: How did the paper get good starting weights?
options: By copying weights from another network
By pretraining one layer at a time on unlabeled data, then fine-tuning the whole network
By setting all weights to zero
By asking humans to choose them
quiz.explain: Each layer learned to model the layer below using restricted Boltzmann machines; then the full stack was fine-tuned with backpropagation.

glossary.definition: A huge dataset of labeled photos organised into thousands of categories. Its yearly challenge used about 1.2 million training images across 1,000 classes.
Graphics processing unit: a chip built for video games that performs thousands of simple calculations in parallel, perfect for neural network maths.
The fraction of test images where the correct label is not among the model's five most confident guesses.
The activation function max(0, z). It is cheap to compute and, unlike the sigmoid, does not flatten out for large positive inputs.
Creating extra training examples by randomly altering existing ones, such as cropping, flipping or shifting colours.
A regularization trick that randomly switches off neurons during training so the network cannot rely too much on any single one.

quiz.q: By roughly how much did AlexNet beat the second-best entry in the 2012 ImageNet challenge (top-5 error)?
options: About 1 percentage point
About 11 percentage points
It tied for first place
It came second
quiz.explain: AlexNet's top-5 error was about 15.3%, compared with about 26.2% for the runner-up, a gap that stunned the computer vision community.

quiz.q: Which of these was NOT one of AlexNet's key ingredients?
options: ReLU activations
Training on GPUs
Hand-designed SIFT features
Dropout and data augmentation
quiz.explain: AlexNet learned its features from raw pixels. Hand-designed features like SIFT were what the competing systems used.

quiz.q: Why did AlexNet use two GPUs?
options: For a backup in case one failed
The network was too large to fit in the memory of a single GPU of that era
One GPU handled training and the other handled testing
Two GPUs were required by the competition rules
quiz.explain: Each GTX 580 had 3 GB of memory, so the network was split across two cards that communicated only at certain layers.

articles.title: Make Your Network Forget, On Purpose
articles.subtitle: Dropout: randomly switching off neurons turns one network into a crowd and stops it from memorizing
articles.paper_title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting

glossary.definition: During training, randomly switching off each neuron with some probability on every step, so the network cannot depend on any single neuron.
When neurons become dependent on each other's specific quirks, forming fragile teams that fit the training data but not new data.
The smaller network that remains after dropout removes some neurons on a given training step.
A collection of models whose predictions are combined, which usually beats any single model.
The chance that a neuron is kept (not dropped) during training, often 0.5 for hidden units and higher for inputs.
Any technique that discourages a model from fitting noise in the training data, so it generalizes better.

quiz.q: What does dropout do during training?
options: Deletes training examples at random
Randomly switches off neurons on each training step
Lowers the learning rate
Removes the last layer
quiz.explain: Each neuron is temporarily removed with some probability, so every step trains a different thinned network.

quiz.q: Why must the weights be adjusted at test time when no neurons are dropped?
options: To make the network slower
Because with all neurons active, each layer would receive more input than it was used to during training
Because test data is different from training data
They do not need adjusting
quiz.explain: If half the neurons were usually off during training, turning them all on doubles the input. Scaling the weights by the retention probability compensates.

quiz.q: In what sense is dropout like training an ensemble?
options: It trains exactly two networks
Each step trains a different thinned network that shares weights, and the full network at test time approximates averaging all of them
It copies the network many times in memory
It only works with random forests
quiz.explain: With n neurons there are 2 to the power n possible thinned networks. Dropout trains them all with shared weights, and the scaled full network approximates their average prediction.

articles.title: The Optimizer Almost Everyone Uses
articles.subtitle: Adam gives every parameter its own smart step size, and became deep learning's default way to walk downhill

glossary.definition: The algorithm that uses gradients to update a model's parameters during training, such as plain gradient descent or Adam.
Keeping a running average of recent gradients so updates build up speed in consistent directions and smooth out noise.
A step size that is adjusted separately for each parameter based on the history of its gradients.
A running average that gives more weight to recent values and gradually forgets old ones.
A fix in Adam that scales up its averages early in training, when they are still dragged toward their starting value of zero.
A setting chosen before training rather than learned, such as the learning rate.

quiz.q: What two ideas does Adam combine?
options: Dropout and batch normalization
Momentum (an average of gradients) and per-parameter scaling by the average squared gradient
Convolution and pooling
Random forests and boosting
quiz.explain: Adam tracks a running mean of gradients (like momentum) and a running mean of squared gradients (like RMSProp), and divides one by the square root of the other.

quiz.q: Why does Adam need bias correction?
options: To remove unfair data
Its running averages start at zero, so early on they underestimate the true values
To speed up the GPU
Because gradients are always biased upward
quiz.explain: With averages initialised to zero, the first few estimates are too small. Dividing by a correction factor fixes this.

quiz.q: What is a practical reason Adam became so popular?
options: It guarantees the global minimum
It works well across many problems with little tuning, often using its default settings
It does not need gradients
It only uses one hyperparameter
quiz.explain: Default values like a learning rate of 0.001 work surprisingly well on many tasks, which saves researchers a lot of trial and error.

articles.title: The Simple Fix That Made Deep Networks Train Fast
articles.subtitle: Batch normalization: keep every layer's inputs well-behaved, and training suddenly gets fourteen times quicker

glossary.definition: Rescaling numbers so they have a standard centre and spread, typically a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
The average of a set of numbers.
A measure of how spread out numbers are around their mean.
The paper's name for the way each layer's input distribution keeps changing during training as earlier layers update.
The small group of training examples processed together in one training step.
An average that is updated step by step during training, used at test time instead of statistics from a single batch.

quiz.q: What does a batch normalization layer do during training?
options: Deletes unusual examples from the batch
Rescales each feature so it has roughly zero mean and unit spread across the mini-batch, then applies a learned scale and shift
Sorts the batch by label
Doubles the learning rate
quiz.explain: It standardises each feature using the batch's own mean and standard deviation, then lets the network learn the best scale and offset.

quiz.q: Why does batch norm include learnable parameters gamma and beta?
options: To make training slower
So the network can undo or adjust the normalization if a different scale works better
To store the labels
They are not needed and are always zero
quiz.explain: Forcing every feature to exactly mean 0 and spread 1 might limit what the layer can express, so gamma and beta restore that freedom.

quiz.q: What does a batch-normalized network use at test time, when there may be just one example?
options: The statistics of the single test example
Running averages of the mean and variance collected during training
Random numbers
It skips the layer entirely
quiz.explain: A single example has no meaningful batch statistics, so the layer uses averages accumulated over training.

articles.title: Why Deeper Got Worse, and the Shortcut That Fixed It
articles.subtitle: ResNet: a one-line change that let networks grow past 100 layers and became the most cited paper of the century

glossary.definition: The surprising finding that adding more layers to a plain deep network can make its training error worse, not better.
The difference between what you want and what you already have. A residual block learns only the change to make to its input.
A shortcut that adds a block's input directly to its output, letting information and gradients bypass the block's layers.
A function that returns its input unchanged. With skip connections, a block can become an identity mapping simply by learning to output zero.
A residual block that shrinks the number of channels, does the expensive work, then expands them again, saving computation in very deep networks.
A deep network made of stacked layers with no skip connections, used in the paper as the comparison.

quiz.q: What surprising problem did the ResNet authors highlight?
options: Deeper plain networks had higher training error than shallower ones
Deeper networks always overfit
GPUs could not run deep networks
Images were too small
quiz.explain: This was not overfitting: the deeper network was worse even on the training data, which meant it was harder to optimize.

quiz.q: What does a residual block compute?
options: Only F(x), ignoring x
F(x) + x, adding the input back to the block's output
x divided by F(x)
A random subset of x
quiz.explain: The block's layers learn a correction F(x), and the skip connection adds the original input x back.

quiz.q: Why do skip connections make very deep networks easier to train?
options: They remove the need for data
A block can easily do nothing by learning zero, and gradients can flow straight back through the shortcuts
They make every layer identical
They reduce the image size
quiz.explain: Learning to output zero is easy, so extra layers cannot easily hurt, and the additive shortcut gives gradients a direct path to early layers.

articles.title: The U-Shaped Network That Learned From Thirty Images
articles.subtitle: U-Net: how a clever shape let a network outline every cell in a microscope image, and later paint pictures
articles.paper_title: U-Net: Convolutional Networks for Biomedical Image Segmentation

glossary.definition: Labeling every pixel of an image with a class, such as cell or background, to produce an exact outline of each object.
The first half of U-Net, which repeatedly shrinks the image while increasing the number of feature channels, capturing what is in the image.
The second half of U-Net, which repeatedly enlarges the feature maps back to full size to say exactly where things are.
In U-Net, a link that copies detailed feature maps from the contracting path directly across to the matching level of the expanding path.
Increasing the width and height of a feature map, for example with a learned transposed convolution.
A data augmentation that randomly and smoothly warps an image, like stretching a rubber sheet, to create realistic new training examples.

quiz.q: What is image segmentation?
options: Giving one label to a whole image
Assigning a label to every pixel, producing exact outlines
Cutting an image into equal squares
Compressing an image
quiz.explain: Classification says 'this image contains a cell'. Segmentation says exactly which pixels belong to which cell.

quiz.q: What do U-Net's skip connections provide?
options: Extra training data
Fine spatial detail from the early layers, so the output can draw precise boundaries
A way to skip training
Random noise
quiz.explain: The contracting path loses detail as it shrinks the image. Skip connections pass that detail directly to the expanding path.

quiz.q: How did U-Net manage to train with so few annotated images?
options: It used millions of unlabeled images
Heavy data augmentation, especially elastic deformations, plus an architecture that uses every pixel as a training signal
It copied labels from another dataset
It did not need training
quiz.explain: Realistic warps of the few labeled images taught the network to be robust to the natural variation of tissue.

articles.title: Teaching Networks to Remember for a Long Time
articles.subtitle: LSTM: gates, a protected memory lane, and the 1997 design that powered speech recognition and translation for two decades
articles.paper_title: Long Short-Term Memory

glossary.definition: A network that reads a sequence one step at a time and passes a hidden state from each step to the next, giving it a form of memory.
The vector a recurrent network carries from one step to the next, summarising what it has read so far.
The way error signals shrink as they are passed back through many steps, so a network cannot learn connections across long gaps.
The LSTM's protected memory lane, which carries information across many time steps with only small, controlled changes.
A set of numbers between 0 and 1, computed by the network, that controls how much information flows through, like a dimmer switch.
The paper's name for the self-connected memory cell whose error signal can loop back through time without shrinking.

quiz.q: What problem was LSTM designed to solve?
options: Images being too large
Recurrent networks forgetting, because error signals vanish over long time gaps
Too much training data
Networks being too fast
quiz.explain: In ordinary recurrent networks, the learning signal shrinks exponentially as it travels back in time, so long-range patterns cannot be learned.

quiz.q: What is the role of the gates in an LSTM?
options: They decide, at each step, how much to write to, keep in, and read from the memory cell
They delete the training data
They speed up the GPU
They choose the learning rate
quiz.explain: Gates are learned dimmer switches: values near 0 block information and values near 1 let it through.

quiz.q: Which gate was NOT in the original 1997 LSTM and was added later?
options: Input gate
Output gate
Forget gate
None, all three were in 1997
quiz.explain: The forget gate, which lets the cell clear old memories, was added by Felix Gers, Schmidhuber and Fred Cummins around 2000.

glossary.definition: A list of a few hundred numbers representing a word, learned so that words with similar meanings get similar vectors.
A learned vector that represents a discrete item, such as a word, as a point in a continuous space.
The few words on either side of a target word that are treated as its neighbours during training.
Continuous bag-of-words: a word2vec model that predicts a missing word from the words around it.
A word2vec model that does the reverse of CBOW: it predicts the surrounding words from a single word.
An evaluation that asks questions like 'man is to king as woman is to what?' and checks if vector arithmetic finds the right word.
A training shortcut from the follow-up paper: instead of scoring every word in the vocabulary, compare the true neighbour against a few random words.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between CBOW and skip-gram?
options: CBOW predicts a word from its neighbours; skip-gram predicts the neighbours from the word
CBOW uses images and skip-gram uses text
Skip-gram has no training
CBOW only works in English
quiz.explain: They are mirror images. Both learn word vectors as a side effect of a simple prediction task.

quiz.q: Why did the authors make their models so simple, with no non-linear hidden layer?
options: Because non-linear layers were not invented yet
So they could train on billions of words quickly, since more data beat a more complex model
Because simple models are always more accurate
Because GPUs cannot run non-linear layers
quiz.explain: Removing the expensive hidden layer made training so cheap that they could use vastly more text, which mattered more for quality.

quiz.q: What does the analogy king - man + woman ≈ queen show?
options: The model memorised a list of royal families
Relationships between words are captured as consistent directions in the vector space
Vectors are random
The model understands grammar rules explicitly
quiz.explain: The difference between king and man points in roughly the same direction as the difference between queen and woman.

articles.title: Read the Whole Sentence, Then Write the Translation
articles.subtitle: Sequence to sequence learning: two LSTMs, one thought vector, and the first neural translator to beat the old guard
articles.paper_title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks

glossary.definition: The network that reads the input sequence and compresses it into a vector.
The network that generates the output sequence, one token at a time, starting from the encoder's vector.
An informal name for the fixed-size vector the encoder produces, meant to capture the meaning of the whole input sentence.
A decoding method that keeps the few most promising partial translations at each step, instead of committing to the single best next word.
A standard machine translation score that measures overlap between a system's output and human reference translations. Higher is better.
The pre-neural approach to translation, built from many separately trained parts such as phrase tables and language models.

quiz.q: How does the seq2seq model translate a sentence?
options: Word by word, looking each word up in a dictionary
An encoder LSTM reads the whole source sentence into a vector, and a decoder LSTM generates the translation from it
It searches the internet for existing translations
It uses hand-written grammar rules
quiz.explain: The encoder compresses the sentence; the decoder unpacks that summary into the other language.

quiz.q: What surprising trick improved results a lot?
options: Translating every sentence twice
Reversing the order of words in the source sentence
Removing all verbs
Using only the first word of each sentence
quiz.explain: Reversing the input put the first source words close to the first target words, creating many short-range dependencies that made learning easier.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of squeezing a sentence into one fixed-size vector?
options: It uses too little memory
Long sentences must be crammed into the same small space, which becomes a bottleneck
It cannot handle the letter e
It makes training too fast
quiz.explain: A single vector has a fixed capacity, which motivated attention mechanisms that let the decoder look back at every input word.

articles.title: The First Time a Network Learned Where to Look
articles.subtitle: Bahdanau attention: letting a translator glance back at the source sentence, and the birth of the most important idea in modern AI
articles.paper_title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate

glossary.definition: A mechanism that lets a model, at each step, compute a weighted mix of all its inputs, putting more weight on the parts that matter most right now.
Which source words correspond to which target words in a translation, such as 'chat' lining up with 'cat'.
The paper's name for the vector the encoder produces for each source word, describing that word in the context of the whole sentence.
Two recurrent networks reading a sentence in opposite directions, so each word's vector reflects both what came before and what comes after.
The weighted average of all source annotations, recomputed for every target word, that the decoder uses to choose its next word.
A function that turns a list of scores into positive weights that add up to 1.

quiz.q: What problem with basic encoder-decoder translation did attention solve?
options: Training was too cheap
Every sentence had to be squeezed into one fixed-size vector, which hurt long sentences
The decoder could not generate words
It only worked for French
quiz.explain: With attention, the decoder no longer depends on a single summary; it can consult every source word's annotation at every step.

quiz.q: How are the attention weights computed for one target word?
options: They are fixed by the programmer
A small network scores each source annotation against the decoder's current state, and a softmax turns the scores into weights
Words are weighted by their length
Only the first source word gets weight
quiz.explain: The scores depend on what the decoder needs right now, so the weights change for every word it produces.

quiz.q: What did the attention weights reveal when visualized?
options: Random noise
Sensible word alignments between the two languages, including reordering, learned without any alignment labels
The training loss
The vocabulary size
quiz.explain: The model learned which source words matched each output word, even where French and English order differ.

articles.title: Teaching an Autoencoder to Dream
articles.subtitle: Variational autoencoders: fuzzy codes, a smooth map of possibilities, and one clever trick that made it trainable
articles.paper_title: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes

glossary.definition: A model that learns the patterns of a dataset well enough to create new examples that look like they came from it.
The hidden space of codes a model uses to describe its data. Points in it correspond to possible outputs.
The distribution the model assumes codes come from before seeing any data, here a simple bell curve centred on zero.
Writing a random sample as a fixed formula plus independent noise, so gradients can flow through the sampling step.
A measure of how different one probability distribution is from another. Zero means they are identical.
The objective a VAE maximizes: how well it reconstructs the data, minus a penalty for codes that stray from the prior. Often called the ELBO.

quiz.q: How does a VAE's encoder differ from a plain autoencoder's?
options: It outputs a single exact code
It outputs a small cloud of possible codes, described by a mean and a spread
It has no weights
It outputs the label of the image
quiz.explain: Each input maps to a distribution over codes. Sampling from it forces nearby codes to decode into similar outputs.

quiz.q: Why is the reparameterization trick needed?
options: To make the model smaller
Because you cannot backpropagate through a random sampling step directly; rewriting it as mean plus spread times noise makes it differentiable
To remove the decoder
To speed up data loading
quiz.explain: With z = mu + sigma times epsilon, the randomness lives in epsilon, and gradients can flow to mu and sigma.

quiz.q: What does the KL term in the VAE objective encourage?
options: Perfect reconstructions at any cost
Codes that stay close to a simple standard bell curve, keeping the latent space smooth and free of holes
Larger images
Fewer training examples
quiz.explain: By pulling every input's code cloud toward the same simple prior, the KL term makes the space continuous, so random points decode to sensible outputs.

glossary.definition: The network in a GAN that turns random noise into fake samples, trying to make them indistinguishable from real data.
The network in a GAN that looks at a sample and outputs the probability that it is real rather than generated.
Training two models against each other, so that each one's improvement forces the other to improve.
A two-player game where one player tries to maximize a score that the other tries to minimize.
A GAN failure where the generator produces only a few kinds of outputs, ignoring much of the variety in the real data.
A list of random numbers fed into the generator. Different noise vectors produce different generated samples.

quiz.q: What does the discriminator in a GAN do?
options: Generates new images
Estimates whether a sample is real data or a fake from the generator
Labels images with their class
Compresses images
quiz.explain: It is the detective: it outputs the probability that its input came from the real dataset.

quiz.q: According to the paper's theory, what happens at the ideal end of training?
options: The discriminator wins and always detects fakes
The generator's samples match the real data distribution, and the discriminator can only guess, outputting one half everywhere
Both networks stop working
The generator copies the training set exactly
quiz.explain: At the theoretical optimum, fakes and real data are indistinguishable, so the best possible detective is a coin flip.

quiz.q: What is mode collapse?
options: The discriminator crashing
The generator producing only a narrow set of outputs instead of the full variety of the data
Training running out of memory
Images becoming too colourful
quiz.explain: A generator can fool the discriminator by perfecting a few outputs, so it stops exploring the full range of real data.

glossary.definition: A generative model that learns to reverse a gradual noising process, turning pure random noise into a realistic sample step by step.
The fixed procedure that adds a little Gaussian noise to an image at each of many steps until only noise remains.
The learned procedure that removes noise step by step, starting from pure noise and ending with a clean image.
Random values drawn from a bell curve, like the static on an old television screen.
The plan for how much noise to add at each step of the forward process.
Fréchet Inception Distance: a score comparing the statistics of generated images with real ones. Lower is better.

quiz.q: What does the network in a diffusion model learn to predict during training?
options: The label of the image
The noise that was added to a noisy image
Whether an image is real or fake
The next pixel from left to right
quiz.explain: Given a noisy image and the step number, the network predicts the noise, which can then be subtracted out.

quiz.q: How do you generate a brand-new image with a trained diffusion model?
options: Start from a random training image
Start from pure random noise and repeatedly apply the learned denoising step
Ask a discriminator to approve it
Decode a single fixed code
quiz.explain: Sampling runs the reverse process: begin with static and remove a little predicted noise at each of many steps.

quiz.q: What was the main practical drawback of the original DDPM?
options: Blurry, low quality images
Unstable adversarial training
Slow sampling, since generating one image took about a thousand network evaluations
It could only generate text
quiz.explain: Quality was excellent, but each sample required running the network once per step, around 1,000 times.

glossary.definition: A compressed representation of images where each image becomes a much smaller grid of numbers that still captures its content.
Shrinking an image while keeping everything that matters to a human viewer, discarding fine pixel-level detail that the eye barely notices.
A pair of networks: an encoder that compresses an image into a small code, and a decoder that rebuilds the image from it.
Attention where one set of things, like image regions, looks up information in another, like the words of a text prompt.
Giving a generative model extra information, such as a caption or a class label, to steer what it creates.
A sampling trick that compares the model's predictions with and without the prompt and pushes further in the prompt's direction, making images follow text more closely.

quiz.q: What is the key efficiency idea of latent diffusion?
options: Use fewer training images
Run the diffusion process on a small compressed representation instead of full-resolution pixels
Skip the denoising network
Generate only black and white images
quiz.explain: An autoencoder first compresses images, so the expensive diffusion steps work on a grid many times smaller.

quiz.q: How does a text prompt steer the image in a latent diffusion model?
options: The text is pasted onto the image
Cross-attention layers inside the denoising U-Net let image regions look up information from the encoded prompt
A human edits each step
The prompt changes the random seed only
quiz.explain: At each denoising step, the network attends to the text encoding, so the words shape what emerges from the noise.

quiz.q: Why does the autoencoder only need to be trained once?
options: Because it is never used
Because the same compressed space can be reused for many diffusion models and tasks
Because it has no parameters
Because images never change
quiz.explain: The compression stage is separate and general, so different diffusion models for different tasks can all share it.

glossary.definition: Learning by trial and error: an agent takes actions in an environment and learns from the rewards it receives.
The learner that observes the environment and chooses actions.
A number the environment gives the agent after an action, such as points in a game. The agent tries to collect as much as possible over time.
An estimate of the total future reward you will get if you take a particular action in a particular situation and play well afterwards.
Storing past experiences in a memory and training on random samples from it, instead of only on the latest moment.
A slowly updated copy of the network used to compute training targets, which keeps learning stable.
Trying actions that are not currently believed to be best, in order to discover better strategies.

quiz.q: What did DQN receive as input when playing Atari games?
options: The game's source code
Raw screen pixels and the game score
Hand-written descriptions of each game
Videos of human experts
quiz.explain: The same network and settings were used for every game, learning only from pixels and score changes.

quiz.q: Why does DQN use experience replay?
options: To save memory
To break the strong correlation between consecutive frames and reuse each experience many times
To watch human replays
To make the game run faster
quiz.explain: Training on random past moments, rather than a stream of nearly identical consecutive frames, makes learning far more stable and data-efficient.

quiz.q: What does a Q-value represent?
options: The quality of the graphics
The expected total future reward of taking an action in a state and acting well afterwards
The number of lives left
The probability of winning immediately
quiz.explain: Q-values look ahead: they include the immediate reward plus discounted future rewards.

glossary.definition: A network that looks at a board position and outputs a probability for each possible move, suggesting which moves are worth considering.
A network that looks at a board position and predicts who is likely to win from there.
A search method that explores possible future move sequences by simulating many games, focusing effort on the most promising lines.
Training a game-playing system by having it play against copies of itself.
All the possible sequences of moves a player could consider. In Go it is astronomically large.
Playing a game out quickly to the end from some position, using a fast simple policy, to estimate who would win.

quiz.q: What did AlphaGo's policy network do?
options: Predict the final score exactly
Suggest which moves are promising in a given position
Count the stones on the board
Choose the board size
quiz.explain: It narrowed the search by giving each legal move a probability, so the program could focus on the few that strong players would consider.

quiz.q: Why was Go considered much harder for computers than chess?
options: Go has more complicated rules
Go has far more possible moves per turn and longer games, and positions are very hard to evaluate
Go is played faster
Computers cannot draw a Go board
quiz.explain: With around 250 legal moves per position and games of about 150 moves, brute-force search is hopeless, and judging who is ahead is subtle.

quiz.q: How was the value network trained?
options: By humans labeling positions
On positions from games AlphaGo played against itself, predicting the eventual winner
By copying a chess engine
It was not trained
quiz.explain: Self-play generated millions of positions with known outcomes, and the network learned to predict the winner from a position.

glossary.definition: The agent's strategy: a function that, given a situation, gives the probability of taking each possible action.
A family of methods that directly adjust the policy, making actions that led to good outcomes more likely.
How much better an action turned out than what the agent expected on average in that situation. Positive means better than expected.
The new policy's probability of an action divided by the old policy's probability. A ratio of 1.2 means the action became 20% more likely.
Limiting a number to a range. PPO clips the probability ratio so a single update cannot change the policy too much.
A zone around the current policy within which updates are considered safe, because the data collected by the old policy still describes them well.

quiz.q: What problem does PPO's clipping solve?
options: Running out of memory
Destructively large policy updates that can collapse performance
Too few actions
Slow GPUs
quiz.explain: If one update changes the policy too much, the agent can suddenly perform terribly. Clipping removes the incentive to move far from the old policy.

quiz.q: If an action had a positive advantage, what does the policy gradient try to do?
options: Make that action less likely
Make that action more likely
Remove the action entirely
Nothing
quiz.explain: Positive advantage means the action worked better than expected, so the policy should choose it more often.

quiz.q: Why was PPO preferred over TRPO by many practitioners?
options: It gave theoretical guarantees TRPO lacked
It achieved similar stability with a much simpler, first-order method that is easy to implement
It does not need any data
It only works on Atari
quiz.explain: TRPO enforced its trust region with complex second-order maths. PPO approximates the same behaviour with a clipped objective and ordinary gradient descent.

glossary.definition: A way for a model to decide which parts of the input matter most for each output, by giving every part a weight and mixing them together.
Attention where every word in a sentence looks at every other word in the same sentence to understand its context.
A small chunk of text, like a word or part of a word, that the model reads as one unit.
An older kind of network that reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a memory forward from each step to the next.
Three vectors made from each token. The query says what a token is looking for, the key says what it offers, and the value is the information it passes on.
A function that turns a list of scores into positive weights that add up to 1, so bigger scores get bigger shares.
Extra numbers added to each token's embedding so the model knows where in the sentence the token sits.
A standard score for machine translation that measures how much a system's output overlaps with human translations. Higher is better.

quiz.q: What did the Transformer remove that earlier translation models depended on?
options: Embeddings
Recurrence, reading words one at a time
The softmax function
Training data
quiz.explain: Transformers process all tokens at once with self-attention instead of stepping through the sentence word by word.

quiz.q: In self-attention, what decides how much one word listens to another?
options: Their distance in the sentence
Alphabetical order
How well the first word's query matches the second word's key
A fixed table written by the researchers
quiz.explain: Each word's query is compared with every key using a dot product. Higher scores become bigger attention weights after the softmax.

quiz.q: Why does the Transformer need positional encodings?
options: To make training slower but more accurate
Because attention on its own has no sense of word order
To translate between languages with different alphabets
To reduce the number of parameters
quiz.explain: Attention treats the input as a set. Without position information, 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would look identical.

glossary.definition: A model that predicts the next token in a piece of text, given the tokens before it.
Training a model on a huge amount of unlabeled data with a general task, like next-word prediction, before adapting it to specific tasks.
Continuing to train a pre-trained model on a smaller labeled dataset for a particular task.
Reusing what a model learned on one task to do better on another, usually with much less data.
A Transformer that keeps only the decoder half, where each token can attend to the tokens before it but not after it.
A chunk of text, often a word or a piece of a word, that the model reads as one unit.
Performing a task without any task-specific training examples.

quiz.q: What task was GPT pre-trained on?
options: Classifying sentiment of movie reviews
Predicting the next token in a large collection of books
Translating English to French
Answering trivia questions
quiz.explain: The model learned language by predicting the next token across thousands of unpublished books, with no labels needed.

quiz.q: How did GPT handle different tasks like entailment or multiple-choice questions?
options: A completely different architecture for each task
By converting each task's inputs into a single sequence of text with special separator tokens, then adding a small output layer
By retraining from scratch for each task
It could not handle them
quiz.explain: Task-specific input formatting let the same pre-trained Transformer handle many tasks with minimal changes.

quiz.q: Which kind of Transformer did GPT use?
options: The full encoder-decoder
Encoder only, reading in both directions
Decoder only, where each token sees only earlier tokens
No Transformer at all
quiz.explain: GPT kept the decoder, with masked attention, which is natural for predicting the next word.

glossary.definition: Able to use context from both the left and the right of a word at the same time.
A pre-training task where some words in a sentence are hidden and the model must predict them from the surrounding words.
BERT's second pre-training task: given two sentences, predict whether the second really follows the first in the original text.
The half of a Transformer where every token can attend to every other token, producing a contextual vector for each one.
Briefly training a pre-trained model on a specific labeled task, usually updating all of its weights.
A vector for a word that depends on the sentence it appears in, so 'bank' in 'river bank' and 'bank loan' get different vectors.

quiz.q: Why couldn't BERT simply be trained to predict the next word, like GPT?
options: Next-word prediction is illegal
With full bidirectional attention, each word could see itself and the answer, so the task would be trivial
BERT has no output layer
Books were not available
quiz.explain: If every word can attend to every other word, predicting the next word is cheating. Masking hides the targets so bidirectional context can be used fairly.

quiz.q: In BERT's masked language model, what happens to the selected 15% of tokens?
options: All are deleted from the sentence
Most become a [MASK] token, some become a random word, and some stay unchanged
They are translated into French
They are moved to the end of the sentence
quiz.explain: 80% become [MASK], 10% a random token and 10% stay the same, so the model cannot rely on always seeing [MASK] during pre-training.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a contextual embedding over a word2vec vector?
options: It uses fewer numbers
The same word gets different vectors depending on its sentence, capturing its meaning in context
It ignores grammar
It only works for nouns
quiz.explain: BERT's output for 'bank' changes with the surrounding words, which resolves ambiguity that a single fixed vector cannot.

glossary.definition: Picking up a task from instructions or examples given in the prompt itself, without any change to the model's weights.
The text you give a language model to continue, which can include instructions and examples.
Giving a model a handful of worked examples of a task in its prompt before asking it to do a new one.
Asking a model to do a task from an instruction alone, with no examples.
One of the learned numbers inside a model. GPT-3 has about 175 billion of them.
When test questions accidentally appear in a model's training data, which can make benchmark scores look better than true ability.

quiz.q: What is in-context learning?
options: Fine-tuning the model's weights on a new dataset
The model picking up a task from examples in its prompt, with no weight updates
Training a model in a classroom
Copying answers from the internet
quiz.explain: GPT-3 was given examples as text in the prompt and continued the pattern, without any gradient updates.

quiz.q: What happened to few-shot performance as model size grew from millions to 175 billion parameters?
options: It stayed flat
It got worse
It improved substantially, and the gap between zero-shot and few-shot widened
It only improved for arithmetic
quiz.explain: Larger models made much better use of examples in context, which is the paper's central finding.

quiz.q: Which of these was a limitation the authors acknowledged?
options: GPT-3 could not write any coherent text
GPT-3 could repeat itself, lose coherence over long passages, and reflect biases in its training data
GPT-3 was too small to be useful
GPT-3 could not answer any questions
quiz.explain: The paper has a long, frank limitations section, including repetition, weak common-sense physics, bias and the cost of training.
